Yes, you can add the fix together with a unit test (integrate(Heaviside(x-1), x, -2, 2)) even if it does not fix the original issue. The rationale for this fix is as follows: Antiderivatives can be computed as Meijer G-functions but they are not necessarily valid on the negative real line. Title: [GSoC] Logarithm bases for `\lg` and `\log`
State: OPEN
Author: wermos
Comments: 20
Body: Background
The ANTLR LaTeX Parser currently parsers \log as base e, and \lg as base 10. While writing the Lark Parser, I wondered how useful this is, because I've only seen \log to denote log base 10, and \lg as the binary logarithm (i.e., log base 2) in computational complexity-related things.
ANTLR cites ISO 80000-2:2019 as its reference for why \lg uses base 10.
When I asked my GSoC mentor @Upabjojr about this, he said that he too believes that \log should use base e.
History
Support for \lg was added in #23618. In that PR, the base for \log was also changed from 10 to $e$, citing the default of the LaTeX printer.
The reasoning given for using \lg to mean was

There seems to be an ISO standard https://en.m.wiktionary.org/wiki/lg#Usage_notes but it’s not widely used in English-language literature. I learned it to be base 10 in China.

But I'm not sure how much weightage we should give to the ISO standards argument, since there is also an ISO standard about typesetting math which says that symbols like e should be upright. However, almost no one in mathematics follows that convention.
Lark Parser
As of right now, I've preserved the ANTLR choice of bases in the Lark rewrite, but once again, I wanted to get the community's thoughts on what base the logarithm should use for both \log and \lg.
Comments:
[1] log should definitely default to base e
For lg, we should try to see what it is actually used as. In general, we should try to match common usage, rather than ISO standards.
[2] log should definitely default to base e

I agree. The reasoning given by @eagleoflqj of matching the default of the LaTeX printer, in addition to the other reasons, is good enough to me.

For lg, we should try to see what it is actually used as. In general, we should try to match common usage, rather than ISO standards.

I agree with this too. Do you have any thoughts on how we might go about this?
[3] Maybe we can try to find uses on arxiv and google scholar. We could at least get an idea of what fields actually use that notation and how they define it.
[4] Maybe we can try to find uses on arxiv and google scholar. We could at least get an idea of what fields actually use that notation and how they define it.

I used this search query on ArXiv, and the search returned two CS papers:

Indexing Graph Search Trees and Applications
Biconnectivity, $st$-numbering and other applications of DFS using $O(n)$ bits

Both papers say

\footnote{We use lg to denote logarithm to the base 2.}

Admittedly, both papers share the same person as first author, so I'll try to look for more evidence for or against $\lg$ as the base 2 logarithm.
Here's another paper that uses the $\lg$ notation to denote the base 2 logarithm. This is the paper that Wikipedia cites for its claim that \lg is also used to denote the base 2 logarithm.
Most notably, this Wikipedia page on the binary logarithm notes that CLRS (a very popular book about Algorithms) uses the $\lg$ notation.
[5] I have always thought of \lg as base 2 logarithm.
I would suggest to create a node for \lg in the Lark parser and then deal with the transformation into the proper logarithm base in the transformer part of the parser. The transformer could have some transformation rules. For example:
In Lark:
LG_NODE: "\lg" expression_mul

In the transformer:
 class TreeToSympy(_lark.Transformer):
    def __init__(self, transformations={"LG_NODE": sympy.log2}):
        self.transformations = transformations

    def LG_NODE(self, token):
        return self.transformations["LG_NODE"](token)
in this way, if a user doesn't like the default interpretation of "\lg", he can pass an alternative dictionary of transformations to the parser.
[6] in this way, if a user doesn't like the default interpretation of "\lg", he can pass an alternative dictionary of transformations to the parser.

This is a good idea, but I think this ties into the more general discussion we should have, which is: What should we leave as user-configurable, and how should we allow for user-configuration in the Lark parser?
I'll open an issue about that soon, so that we can start discussing how to this issue, along with a few other related issues.
[7] User configurability is indeed something that I'm hopeful we can get a lot of with the Lark parser. Even so, we should have good defaults so that the majority of users don't have to worry about it.
[8] I just expect that user configurable functions to have type annotations, and to be discussed about type safety
[9] @sylee957 can you clarify what you mean? How do you imagine the user configurability for the latex parser to look like?
Personally I see two types of configurability. One is changing the meaning of an existing parsed node, like changing \lg to parse as log(x) instead of log(x, 2). That could probably just be done by passing a dictionary to parse_latex. The second would be for the user to extend the grammar itself to be able to parse things that aren't otherwise parsable. I'm not sure yet what that should look like, and it probably depends on the implementation details of how Lark works. Maybe @Upabjojr has ideas here.
[10] But at any rate, I'm not clear how type safety factors in.
[11] I expect users to know what the *** is input and output of LG_NODE it is.
The best way to do this is by type system, and the worst is by expecting the users to read the source code, even though it is open source.
And even from the library, if you expect things are guaranteed to be str, Expr or such, it is more easier to trust what users give. And users should be able to trust the library if they are designed to be working uniformly for a certain functional type.
[12] And i also recommend to factor out your own grammar in modules,
https://lark-parser.readthedocs.io/en/stable/grammar.html#import
with its module system before getting an insight about how user-configurable grammar itself should look like.
I can share some tricks for more tricky refactory, like factoring out recursive grammar (like arithmetic), which I had used to do before at work.
I’d like to factor out the things like trigonometry, functions, numbers, greek, … into separate modules because having one big expression grammar file often ends up with a mess.
[13] @sylee957 thanks for the tips. If you want to be more involved in the project you can join the Matrix chat https://matrix.to/#/#sympy-gsoc-2023-latex-parser:matrix.org (we can also add you to the weekly video calls if you are interested). Having someone who's worked with this stuff before would indeed be helpful.
[14] I'm a little unsure about typing. The only way to know what type an expression node will really support is to create it, because SymPy nodes themselves are not really typed well enough to check that. I think we'd want to have SymPy itself be typed before we can heavily type the parser. And in LaTeX, you can in principle create anything, even nonsense that doesn't make any sense type-wise, but there'd be no way to know that it is nonsense until you try to create the SymPy expression. If anything, I'd think the parser nodes should not be typed, and just represent structurally whatever the user input, and let the actual typing and representation of semantic mathematical meaning come after translating it to SymPy.
[15] It can be possible not to type, however, in that regards, you should make the options to be very simple, not more than boolean or string flags.

[17] The only way to know what type an expression node will really support is to create it, because SymPy nodes themselves are not really typed well enough to check that.

Title: Jupyter notebook LaTeX output breaks when processed in LaTeX, ironically
State: CLOSED
Author: mgeier
Comments: 12
Body: Steps to reproduce:


Create a Jupyter notebook (named, say, mynotebook.ipynb) with this content:
import sympy as sp
sp.init_printing()
1


Convert it to LaTeX (you can remove the --execute flag if you saved the result in the notebook):
python3 -m nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --execute --to pdf



This creates the error (originating from LaTeX):
...
! LaTeX Error: Bad math environment delimiter.

See the LaTeX manual or LaTeX Companion for explanation.
Type  H <return>  for immediate help.
 ...                                              
                                                  
l.300     $$\begin{equation*}
                             1\end{equation*}$$
? 
! Emergency stop.
 ...                                              
                                                  
l.300     $$\begin{equation*}
                             1\end{equation*}$$
...

If you only convert --to latex, you'll see that this LaTeX code is generated:
...
\texttt{\color{outcolor}Out[{\color{outcolor}1}]:}
    
    $$\begin{equation*}1\end{equation*}$$
...
The reason for this error message is that the equation* environment is meant to be used in text mode, but sandwiching the whole thing between $$ switches to math mode.
In this case the $$ should simply be removed, but a general solution to this problem might be more involved.
Comments:
[1] I wonder if this change #15367 caused this.
[2] Looks like it.
Please note that using a math environment (like equation*) is a step into the wrong direction, see #15329.
[3] I've created PR #15625 to fix this.
[4] Ouch I didn't realize this broke nbconvert. We should definitely get this fixed before releasing. I wonder if we should add a test to the test suite that executes and nbconverts a simple SymPy notebook.
[5] Yeah, I guess such a test would be good.
You could also consider moving the notebooks from the examples/ directory to your docs.
This way they could be automatically executed (using my little nbsphinx extension) whenever the documentation is built. You could then make building the docs part of the CI tests.
And when generating the PDF of the docs, this error here would be spotted.
[6] Actually we don't even ship the notebooks, the main reason being that we don't have automated testing for them. So I agree moving them to the docs and rendering them as part of the tests would be good.
[7] I was pointed to https://github.com/computationalmodelling/nbval as a way to test the output of notebooks (apparently it's also not hard to do manually, see https://twitter.com/SylvainCorlay/status/1074744629512286215).
[8] There was discussion some time back about where notebooks belong. This was created but never populated:
https://github.com/sympy/sympy-notebooks
An then this was created separately:
https://github.com/sympy/quantum_notebooks
One key thing is that we wouldn't want to commit notebooks with outputs or have to host image binaries in the main sympy directory.
It is easy enough to execute the notebooks on travis with something like:
jupyter nbconvert --debug --ExecutePreprocessor.enabled=True --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=300 --to=html nb.ipynb
[9] Yeah but the problem with just executing the notebooks is that it doesn't check that the output stays the same. Ideally it would also test the output, like we do for doctests.
I agree if a notebook has any kind of image output it should note be stored in this repo.
[10] Yes, sure. The command I posted is better than not running them at all, and checking the output is even better. The former is pretty low overhead to setup as an initial "test".
[11] The error in this issue occurred during the LaTeX run, so the nbconvert command would have to use --to=pdf to detect this error.
I guess nbval doesn't help in this case, because it looks at the output in the notebook file as opposed to the resulting HTML/LaTeX/PDF file, right?
My main question about the notebooks is: do you want their contents to be part of the documentation or not?
If yes, you should consider using nbsphinx.
If not, but you want to use them as regression tests, you should consider using nbval.
Theoretically, you could also do both. But I guess the content of the notebooks should very much depend on whether they are used as part of the user documentation or as part of the automated tests.
[12] No, we would have to test that separately. My point about nbval is that if we have rendered notebooks in the docs, then we should actually test the output of the notebook cells, the same as we do with doctests. The point of doctests isn't to be regression tests (we have normal tests for that). They should rather be thought of as documentation that happens to be tested. It tests that the output of the documentation examples is actually what it says that it is, and if changes, we are aware of it and it gets updated. Sometimes this catches actual regressions as well, but that's not the point of it. I see something like nbval filling the same role as doctests for example notebooks.
